title: Effectiveness of a Generate–Verify–Repair Pipeline with Batfish for LLM‑Generated Vendor CLI Configurations
abstract: We report a preregistered paired experiment (cnsms2026-001-gvr-batfish-prereg-v1; preregistration manifest SHA‑256: 46a223492f760950b3d06f475129ce21e52e296c4c2a1e09df3ccd50bec9f891) that evaluated whether a generate–verify–repair (GVR) pipeline—shared initial LLM candidate (gpt-5-mini) + deterministic Batfish‑style validator + at most one automated LLM repair—reduces deterministic‑verifier detected semantic/safety failures on intent→vendor‑CLI tasks. Planned N=300 task pairs; 266 complete pairs were analysed after preregistered exclusions. Baseline pass-rate = 260/266 (97.744%); guarded (final GVR) pass-rate = 265/266 (99.624%). Paired difference = 0.01879699248; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 0.0625. The exact McNemar test was the preregistered primary decision procedure; a paired bootstrap (B=10,000; seed=1729) CI = [0.0037593985, 0.0375939850] is presented as a supplementary descriptive interval and does not replace the preregistered test. Repair was invoked for 6 tasks; median repair iterations per task = 0. Per‑episode latency was not archived and thus could not be evaluated. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics the observed absolute improvement is small and did not meet the preregistered α=0.05 decision rule. We archive raw model outputs, validator traces, reconciliation and provider accounting artifacts, representative repaired episodes, and the immutable initial master prompt reference for auditability.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are actively explored for NetOps tasks such as intent→CLI translation, zero‑touch configuration synthesis, and automated maintenance workflows [1]. Stochastic LLM outputs can produce syntactic errors, missing or misordered commands, or semantic constraint violations (e.g., transiently bringing redundant interfaces down) that create operational risk if applied directly. To mitigate this risk, pipelines that interpose deterministic verifiers (e.g., Batfish or header‑space analyses) and bounded automated repair loops—collectively generate–verify–repair (GVR)—have been proposed to provide a deterministic acceptance criterion and automated correction [3,4]. Prior work describes components and prototypes, but preregistered, paired evaluations that archive verifier traces and quantify verifier‑triggered repair benefit on reproducible NetOps task banks are limited.

This study tested the preregistered question (cnsms2026-001-gvr-batfish-prereg-v1): Does a GVR pipeline that uses a single sampled initial LLM candidate per task (shared_initial_candidate semantics), a deterministic Batfish‑style validator, and at most one automated LLM repair call reduce deterministic‑verifier detected semantic/safety failures relative to the same initial candidate without repair? Our principal contribution is a preregistered, artifact‑archived paired evaluation executed under the CNSM Agentic AI Researcher constraints that reports exact paired counts, inferential outcomes, execution accounting, representative artifact‑grounded repair examples, and an evidence‑grounded interpretation.
sections.related_work:
LLM applications in NetOps span intent‑to‑configuration translation, automated configuration generation, and AIOps toolchains; recent benchmark and survey efforts document both capability and failure modes [1,2]. NetConfEval‑style work shows vendor‑specific syntax, sequencing, and ordering constraints remain failure points for unconstrained generation [1]. Broader surveys report hallucination and constraint‑violation risks and recommend grounding, verifier integration, and tooling to reduce operational risk [2].

Generate–verify–repair (GVR) architectures are proposed in code generation and regulated‑document contexts to combine stochastic generators with deterministic oracles and bounded repairs; these proposals outline desiderata for reproducible verifiable outputs from stochastic agents [3]. Deterministic network verifiers (Batfish and header‑space analyses) provide automatable checks for reachability, ordering, and policy constraints; however, verifier rule coverage and engineering tradeoffs shape practical effectiveness [4]. Our study differs by executing the preregistered paired test under shared_initial_candidate semantics, archiving detailed validator traces, and reporting exact paired contingency counts together with the preregistered exact McNemar test and a supplementary paired bootstrap CI for effect magnitude.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: The experiment followed the preregistered plan cnsms2026-001-gvr-batfish-prereg-v1 (manifest SHA‑256: 46a223492f760950b3d06f475129ce21e52e296c4c2a1e09df3ccd50bec9f891). The primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Under these semantics the identical single sampled initial model candidate per task is used to produce both outcomes: (1) baseline — score the single initial candidate with the deterministic validator; (2) guarded — if that same candidate fails, the pipeline may invoke at most one automated LLM repair call and then rescore with the same deterministic validator. The shared_initial_candidate design isolates the verifier‑triggered repair effect for a fixed initial draw; it does not measure the effect of constrained prompting, multiple independent draws, or ensemble first‑pass generation.

Primary inferential procedure and interval reporting: The preregistered primary hypothesis test was the exact McNemar two‑sided test on paired binary outcomes at α=0.05 (estimator id paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline). We report that exact two‑sided McNemar p‑value as the preregistered decision statistic. The paired bootstrap percentile CI (B=10,000 resamples; seed=1729) reported in Results is included as a supplementary descriptive interval estimator; it is explicitly supplementary and was not used to overturn the preregistered McNemar decision.

Task bank, sampling, and inclusion rules: A deterministic task generator produced N=300 intent→CLI pairs stratified into two vendor‑dialect clusters (150 Cisco‑like, 150 Juniper‑like) using seeded generation as specified in the preregistration. Inclusion and exclusion rules followed the preregistered contract: exact public duplicates (per contamination checks) would be excluded from primary analysis (none were excluded by exact duplication), and provider/API transient failures triggered up to two automatic retries. Pairs where both arms failed due to infrastructure/model API errors were excluded from the primary paired analysis per the preregistered 'complete_pair_primary' rule. Applying those preregistered exclusions produced 266 complete pairs analysed (see deterministic_reconciliation artifact; SHA‑256: 32ea4be9caac88b78993caafec4ac323b8b822f1b6813e0e3747f3144e7a4490), with both_missing_pairs = 34 excluded under the preregistered rule.

Model orchestration, provider accounting, and stage semantics: The declared model used for generation and any repair calls was gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json declared_model_version = "gpt-5-mini"). Execution artifacts record provider and stage accounting and we clarify their operational meaning here. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics a single "shared_initial_generation" model call was produced per task (one sampled candidate) and that same shared candidate was evaluated for both baseline and guarded outcomes; stage_counts.shared_initial_generation = 300 in the reconciled accounting. The guarded condition does not imply an independent full generation for the guarded arm; instead, additional model calls recorded under the "repair" stage are the bounded repair invocations invoked only when the shared initial candidate failed the validator. Deterministic reconciliation/provider audit records show hosted_model_call_event_count = 306 total model‑call events, completed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 272, failed_hosted_model_call_event_count = 34, and stage_counts: {"shared_initial_generation": 300, "repair": 6}. The reconciled condition_counts (shared = 300, guarded = 6) in provider accounting therefore indicate model‑call staging counts, not independent per‑arm full‑generation counts; this distinction preserves the shared_initial_candidate estimand and is required by the preregistered execution contract (generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate").

Deterministic validator and scoring: A deterministic oracle (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) executed a fixed rule battery archived per episode: (1) CLI syntactic parsing and normalization; (2) required‑sequence checks against the task's required_sequence; (3) constrained‑field touch checks against allowed_touched_fields and allowed_fields; (4) reachability/constraint validation over the deterministic synthetic topology (Batfish‑style). Each episode archives validation_before and validation_after records containing parsed_command_count, required_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, violation codes, normalized_configuration, and boolean valid. The primary binary endpoint used the preregistered 'full_intent_constraint_validation' scoring rule. Repair prompts include the task constraints, validator failure diagnostics, and an instruction to produce a corrected configuration respecting the same constraints; repair calls were bounded to ≤1 per failing episode by design.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and sample flow: Planned_episode_count = 600 (300 pairs × 2 arms). Completed_episode_count = 532; failed_episode_count = 68 due to provider/infrastructure events. Applying the preregistered 'complete_pair_primary' exclusion rule (exclude both‑arm provider failures) produced complete_pairs = 266 for the primary confirmatory analysis; both_missing_pairs = 34 were excluded (deterministic_reconciliation.json SHA‑256: 32ea4be9caac88b78993caafec4ac323b8b822f1b6813e0e3747f3144e7a4490).

Primary paired outcomes: For the 266 complete pairs the validator contingency counts were: n11 = 260 (both baseline and guarded pass), n10 = 5 (guarded pass only), n01 = 0 (baseline pass only), n00 = 1 (both fail). These produce baseline_success_rate = 260/266 = 0.9774436090 and guarded_success_rate = 265/266 = 0.9962406015; paired (guarded − baseline) difference = 0.01879699248. The preregistered exact McNemar two‑sided test on discordants (n10 = 5, n01 = 0) yields p = 0.0625, which does not meet the preregistered α = 0.05 rejection threshold.

Interval estimate and supplementary summary: The paired bootstrap percentile CI (B = 10,000 resamples; seed = 1729) for the paired difference is [0.0037593985, 0.0375939850]. We present this bootstrap CI as a descriptive measure of effect magnitude and sampling variability; it is supplementary to (not a replacement for) the preregistered exact McNemar decision. The small discordant count (total discordants = 5) creates discreteness in the exact test that can make the two‑sided p conservative for small effects while the bootstrap CI captures resampled paired‑difference variability.

Repair invocation and yield: Repair calls were invoked in 6 episodes (stage_counts.repair = 6). Among analysed pairs the discordant pattern (n10 = 5, n01 = 0) indicates that up to five repair invocations converted a failing shared initial candidate into a guarded pass in the analysed set; at most one repair among complete pairs did not produce a guarded pass. Median repair iterations per analysed task = 0 (most tasks did not require repair). Total model_calls_used recorded = 306; completed model calls = 272; failed model calls = 34 (provider accounting archived).

Derived descriptive scalar (NNT): Interpreting the paired absolute risk reduction descriptively yields an approximate number‑needed‑to‑treat (NNT) = 1 / 0.01879699248 ≈ 53.2; i.e., under these run conditions roughly 53 guarded tasks were associated with one additional verifier‑approved configuration relative to baseline. This NNT is descriptive and conditional on the high baseline pass rate and shared_initial_candidate semantics.

Representative repair diagnostics: Representative archived episodes illustrate typical failures and repairs. For example, task-000008 (difficulty = "extreme") had a truncated final line in the shared initial candidate and failed parsed_command_count vs required_command_count checks; an automated repair call produced a completed final command sequence and the guarded final validator trace recorded validation_after.valid = true and violation_count = 0. Per‑episode validator traces record the specific violation codes and normalized_configuration to enable audit and targeted analysis of repair logic and validator coverage.

Sensitivity to missingness: Thirty‑four both‑arm episodes were excluded from the primary analysis per the preregistered 'complete_pair_primary' rule; inclusion of those 34 episodes as failures in a conservative sensitivity treatment changes per‑condition proportions (baseline = 260/300, guarded = 265/300) but does not alter the discordant counts (n10 = 5, n01 = 0) producing the same exact McNemar p = 0.0625 on the analysed pairs. All exclusions and reconciling counts are archived in deterministic_reconciliation.json (SHA‑256 above).
sections.discussion:
Statistical interpretation and small‑discordant behavior: The guarded GVR pipeline produced a small absolute improvement (~1.88 percentage points). The preregistered exact McNemar test did not reject at α=0.05 (p = 0.0625). The paired bootstrap CI that excludes zero is a supplementary descriptive indicator of a small positive effect; with few discordants the exact discrete test can be conservative while bootstrap resampling reflects observed paired‑difference variability. We therefore present both inferential views and emphasize the preregistered McNemar decision as the primary confirmatory result.

Operational implications grounded in artifacts: Baseline first‑pass accuracy was high (≈97.7%), leaving few failures for repair and yielding infrequent repair invocations (6/300). Stage and provider accounting (hosted_model_call_event_count = 306; repair = 6; shared_initial_generation = 300) show that the GVR pipeline invoked relatively few additional model calls in this corpus. However, because per‑episode latency was not archived in per‑task artifacts, end‑to‑end timing and latency bounds could not be evaluated, and therefore operational latency tradeoffs remain unmeasured in this run.

Threats to validity (artifact‑grounded): Internal validity: shared_initial_candidate semantics measure the effect of validator‑triggered repair for a fixed initial sample and do not support claims about alternative interventions such as constrained first‑pass prompting or multiple independent draws. Construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces a finite rule battery; semantic violations outside its coverage are unmeasured. External validity: the task corpus uses public NetConfEval‑style examples plus a seeded synthetic generator limited to two vendor clusters; results may not generalize to other vendors, larger topologies, or production heterogeneity. Conclusion validity: the loss of 34 both‑arm provider failures reduced effective N and limited power to detect small absolute differences.

Design lessons and recommendations: (1) When baseline pass rates are high, experiments should target corpora with lower first‑pass accuracy or include independent generation arms to increase discordant counts and power. (2) Archive per‑episode latency instrumentation to enable evaluation of operational latency bounds. (3) Expand and publish validator rule coverage and include auditor tests for verifier false negatives. (4) Consider separate preregistered arms to compare shared_initial_candidate semantics to independent generation semantics; those contrasts require independent initial draws and were outside this run's scope.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired experiment evaluating a GVR pipeline (gpt‑5‑mini + deterministic_netops_validator_v5 + ≤1 automated repair) under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Across 266 analysed pairs the guarded pipeline improved validator pass rate by 0.01879699248 but did not meet the preregistered exact‑McNemar α=0.05 decision rule (p=0.0625); a paired bootstrap CI (B=10,000, seed=1729) is reported as a supplementary descriptive interval and narrowly excludes zero. Repair calls were rare (6/300) and median repair iterations per task = 0. Per‑episode latency was not archived and thus the preregistered latency estimand could not be assessed. All execution and analysis artifacts (raw responses, validator traces, provider call accounting, and reconciliation manifests) are archived to support reanalysis and follow‑on work.

limitations: Shared_initial_candidate semantics: both arms used the same single sampled initial candidate per preregistration; the estimand measures validator‑triggered repair benefit for that fixed initial sample and does not evaluate independent first‑pass generations or constrained first‑pass prompting strategies.

Missingness and sample reduction: planned N=300 pairs; after infrastructure/provider exclusions 266 pairs were complete and 34 both‑arm episodes were excluded per preregistered rules, reducing effective sample size and precision.
Small discordant counts: primary inference used exact McNemar with few discordants (n10=5, n01=0); conclusions are sensitive to inferential choice and limited power.
Validator coverage: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces a finite set of syntactic/semantic/reachability rules; semantic violations outside its coverage are possible and unmeasured.

Runtime nondeterminism and sampling: archived execution/model_configuration.json records temperature = null and no deterministic seed; nondeterministic sampling cannot be excluded for recorded model calls.
H2 latency not evaluated: per‑episode end‑to‑end latency was not present in archived per‑task artifacts and therefore the preregistered latency bound (median ≤ 60 s) could not be assessed.

External validity: task corpus derives from public NetConfEval‑style examples and a seeded synthetic generator limited to two vendor‑dialect clusters; results do not imply universal benefit across other vendors, larger topologies, or production deployments.
